source.title: How Width and Data Shape Generalization Scaling Laws in Quadratic Neural Networks
source.authors: Julius Girardin; Emanuele Troiani; Yi-Zhou Xu; Vittorio Erba; Florent Krzakala; Lenka Zdeborová

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper derives and numerically checks scaling laws for excess test error in a finite-width quadratic network. It finds multiple width-dependent regimes, including increasing and decreasing error, and cautions that its precise exponents do not transfer directly to realistic deep architectures. This refines the scope of scaling-law claims but is not a test on language models.
record.gate_note: The study measures excess test error in a synthetic quadratic-network ERM setting, not held-out language-model cross-entropy. Results from cited works are not recorded. The numerical agreement between the paper's theory and its own optimization runs is part of its evidence.
record.test_reason: The study derives, and checks against its own LBFGS training runs, how excess test error scales with width and sample count. The setting is a synthetic, feature-learning quadratic two-layer network trained by ℓ2-regularized ERM. This is a new, non-language-model setting with its own scaling results, so it bears on V5 (power-law form beyond LM pretraining) and on V7's 'curves bend away from a single power law'. It does not test V1–V4 or V6, which concern LM pretraining loss, compute allocation, architecture shape and downstream tasks. The scaling exponents come from a heuristic replica-symmetric, non-asymptotic state-evolution analysis, not from fits to training runs. Training runs at d=400–800 agree with the theory, but the authors say the exponents need not transfer to realistic deep architectures.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially correct. In this stylized quadratic feature-learning model, sample size, width, regularization and target spectrum jointly set excess test error. Width-wise curves show several phases: power-law decay, overfitting rise, post-interpolation decay, plateau and an interpolation peak. Limited width acts as an implicit regularizer, and optimal width, optimal regularization or pruning each reach Bayes-optimal rates. The authors do not claim the exponents transfer to realistic deep architectures.
record.recipe_differences: A synthetic, shallow quadratic network trained by regularized ERM on Gaussian inputs with square loss, rather than language-model pretraining measured by held-out cross-entropy.
record.method_sensitivity: The scaling regimes and exponents depend on sample scaling α, width scaling ρ, regularization scaling ℓ, and target spectral exponent γ; the optimal width can also depend on label-noise level Δ.

fits_no_version.finding: Width acts as an implicit regularizer. Choosing the optimal width, tuning ℓ2 regularization optimally, or pruning after training each reaches the Bayes-optimal sample-wise rate n^{-1+1/2γ}.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In feature-learning models, a finite-width constraint can regularize as well as optimal explicit regularization, at the level of scaling exponents.

record.problems: The main scaling equations are a replica-symmetric, non-asymptotic extension whose rigorous justification is explicitly open. The rank-constrained problem is non-convex, and optimization is not guaranteed to reach the global minimum. Numerical experiments use finite dimensions; reported standard deviations are over at least two realizations.

untested.parts: Real other modalities (image, video), repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer; any real-data or deep-network setting.
How parameter counting, training schedule or fitting method change published exponents, and compute-optimal splits; no empirical power-law fits are compared.

missing.what: Interpolation (double-descent) peak in test error versus width, exponent β=−(2/3)ℓ+(ρ−1)/3 at α=ρ+1.
missing.locator: Appendix B.1 Case IV, Eq. 118; Fig. 7

missing.what: Sample-wise scaling at optimal width reaching the Bayes-optimal rate n^{-1+1/2γ}.
Discontinuous jump in the scaling exponent at ρ=1 when α>1+2γ: d^{-2γ} below versus d^{2-α} above.
Noiseless (Δ=0) phase diagram: error decays as p^{1-2γ}, then plateaus after p=n/d.
Optimal-regularization error scaling (Eq. 16) and post-training pruning rates.

record.verdict_notes: Analytic heuristic study (replica-symmetric state evolution, rigorous proof open) with numerical LBFGS checks; no language models. All rows are theoretical scaling predictions, so their states describe the predicted behaviour. V5 linkage is a judgement call: the setting is a toy training regime, not one of the real modalities V5 names. The V7 verdict covers only the 'bends away from a single power law' and setup-dependence parts, not fitting-method disagreements.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model pretraining cross-entropy and its scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits to small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
The allocation of parameters and tokens under a fixed compute budget; the paper studies width and sample count, not compute-optimal language-model training.
Comparisons of depth, width, or architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study tests scaling in a synthetic quadratic-network ERM setting, but not other modalities, language models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream task performance and its predictability from pretraining loss.
The study does not compare language-model exponent fits or compute-optimal splits across the original studies' parameter-counting, data, and schedule choices.

rows.note: The paper reports this power-law width dependence for the stylized quadratic-network setting.
rows.check: The value is a theoretical prediction (Result 2, Eq. 10), not a measured fit; it is supported numerically at d=400–800 (Figs 1, 3). Width-wise decay follows p^{1-2γ}.

rows.subject: quadratic two-layer neural network
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical excess-test-error scaling with network width and sample count
rows.note: In this phase the error increases with width, attributed to fitting noise-dominated directions.
rows.check: For V5 the error grows with width here (overfitting label noise), the opposite of loss falling with parameters. 'observed' is right only as a description of the phase, not of the version. Condition per Eq. 90: 1+2γρ>α>1+ρ, ℓ<α/2−1.

source_check.correct: For the noisy setting Δ>0, require (α−1)/(2γ)<ρ<min(1,α−1), α<1+2γ, and ℓ<α/2−1. E=Θ(d^{ρ−α+1}). State: reversed for V5; observed for V7.
source_check.locator_found: Result 2, Eq. (10), second branch; Appendix B.1, Case II, Eqs. (89)–(90).
source_check.problem: The explicit inequalities omit ρ<1; reversed describes V5 but does not describe the linked V7 effect.

rows.subject: quadratic two-layer neural network
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical excess-test-error scaling with network width and sample count
rows.note: The paper describes this phase as decreasing error with increasing width after interpolation.
rows.check: Theoretical decreasing power law in width after interpolation. Condition per Eq. 95 is narrower than 'α<2': it also requires ρ<α−1 and α above a γ-dependent bound.

source_check.correct: For Δ>0, require 1<α<2, α−1<ρ<ρeff,1(α,γ), and ℓ<α/2−1. E=Θ(d^{α−ρ−1}). Appendix Eq. (95) gives 1+ρ>α>max(1+2γρ/(4γ−1),(5ρ+1)/3).
source_check.problem: α<2 alone does not identify this phase; the pack's verdict-fix assertion ρ<α−1 reverses the required inequality.

rows.subject: quadratic two-layer neural network
rows.note: The plateau is independent of width once the effective-rank threshold is exceeded.
rows.check: The error is flat in width, but here width is not the bottleneck: it exceeds the effective target rank. In samples it scales as d^2/n, a power law, so 'observed' holds for the sample-wise law. For V7 the row shows the curve bending from a width power law to a plateau.

source_check.locator_found: Result 2, Eqs. (10)–(12): α>2 gives ϕ1=2−α and ρeff,1=1; full-width discussion.

rows.subject: quadratic two-layer neural network
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical excess-test-error scaling with width under stronger regularization
rows.note: The paper reports a low-width power law followed by a width-independent plateau.
rows.check: Theoretical prediction, supported numerically (Fig. 3 left, Fig. 5). The condition also needs α>ℓ+3/2.

rows.subject: quadratic two-layer neural network
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical excess-test-error scaling in the rank-collapse regime
rows.note: The paper states that the fitted network weights collapse to zero in this regime.
rows.check: Error stays at order one (weights collapse to zero), so no scaling occurs in this regime. The record's 'observed' describes the phase, not the version's effect.

source_check.correct: E∼1 and the ERM weights collapse to zero when α<max(1,ℓ+3/2). State: absent for V5; observed for V7.
source_check.locator_found: Section 2, regime definitions and rank-collapse paragraph.
source_check.problem: Absent describes the decreasing-error effect of V5; this conditional plateau supports the linked V7 effect.

relationships.reason: Excess error follows power laws in width (R1, R3, R5) and in samples (R4, d^{2-α}), matched by LBFGS runs at d=400–800.
relationships.display_finding: Excess error follows width and sample power laws across the studied phases, matching LBFGS simulations at dimensions 400–800.
